title.en: Sarabha-miga-Jātaka (The Stag That Saved the King)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Benares and the royal hunting forest

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A hunting king, mocked by his courtiers for missing a stag, chases it alone into the forest and falls into a sixty-cubit pit; the stag he hunted hauls him out without a thought of malice and teaches him the Five Virtues. When Sakka tests the king by tempting him to shoot the stag that appears at his target, the king refuses—'this very stag saved me from hopeless woe'—and Sakka reveals himself and blesses his mercy.
summary.zh: 王獵鹿不中，為群臣所笑，遂單身逐鹿入林，墮六十肘深坑；所逐之鹿不念舊惡，援王出坑，並教以五戒。後帝釋化樹靈試王，誘其射鹿，王言「此鹿嘗救我於絕境」，堅拒之；帝釋現身讚其仁而賜福。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living Buddhist tradition; freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this in the Hall of Truth to show Sāriputta's wisdom, after the miracle at Sāvatthī where a mango stone planted at the city gate grew before the crowd's eyes into a tree a hundred cubits tall; the quarrelsome sectarians were confounded, and the Teacher, ascending to the Heaven of the Thirty-three for the rains, returned by a stairway of gems, silver and gold at Sankassa, and there, by a ladder of graded questions, made known before all men and gods the greatness of the Captain of the Faith. "This is not the first time," said he, "that Sāriputta answered at large a question briefly put." Of old, when Brahmadatta was king of Benares, the Bodhisatta lived in the forest as a stag; the king delighted in hunting and reckoned no other man worthy of the name.

One day in the hunt the king declared that whoever let a deer pass should be punished, and the courtiers, posting him at the end of a path, drove a great covert toward him. Our stag was first to be put up; seeing men in an unbroken ring on every side, he saw his only chance where the king stood, and rushed at him with eyes dazzling like flung sand. The king shot and missed—the deer are clever to dodge arrows—and the stag, swift as the wind, broke through the circle. The courtiers made sport of their king without stint: "He has hit the ground!" Stung by their mockery, the king girded up his loins and chased the stag on foot, sword in hand, for three leagues. The stag sniffed the smell of water in a sixty-cubit pit hidden under weeds and swerved aside; the king went straight on and fell in. Hearing no footsteps, the stag turned, saw his peril, and pitied rather than hated him.

"Fear nothing, O king, for I will deliver you from your distress," cried the stag from the pit's edge, and with an effort as earnest as though he were saving his own beloved son he braced himself on the rock and hauled the king out of the deep pit, set him on his back, and carried him forth from the forest. There he admonished the king and established him in the Five Virtues; the king begged him to come to Benares and rule it, but the stag answered that he was one of the animals and wanted no kingdom—let the king keep the precepts he had taught, and teach them to his subjects. The king went home weeping to remember the stag's nobility, proclaimed by the drum of the Law that all the city should observe the five virtues, and at daybreak sat cross-legged and chanted his aspiration in six stanzas—"Hope on, O man, if thou be wise..." The chaplain, come thus early to enquire after the king's welfare, overheard the chant and deduced the whole adventure as clearly as a face in a polished mirror, and told it back to the astonished king, who gave him a rich present.

One day the king went into the park with the chaplain to shoot at a mark, and Sakka, perceiving how the king's virtue was filling heaven with new sons and daughters of the gods, resolved to try him. By his power he made the stag appear at the target, and entering the chaplain's body urged him: let fly the shaft, for the stag is meat for monarchs. "I am grateful for a service done, and therefore hold my hand from killing now," the king replied. Then Sakka threatened: kill it, a Titan, not a stag, and thou shalt be king of the gods; refuse, and thou and wife and children shall descend to death's cold river. "So be it," answered the king; "by my hand this stag shall not be slain. That very stag saved me from hopeless woe—how can I wish my benefactor dead?" Sakka left the chaplain's body and stood in the air in his own shape, blessing the true and faithful friend—"comfort with truth and goodness this domain, and thou shalt reign as Indra amid the gods"—then returned. Of that time Ananda was the king, Sariputta the chaplain, and the Master the stag.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Mountain of the Moon (Canda-pabbata) in the Himalaya (symbolic pin)

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: The Bodhisatta, born a kinnara or woodland fairy, and his wife Canda live in loving song on the Mountain of the Moon. A king on a solitary hunting trip shoots the fairy out of lust for his wife; Canda curses the king, refuses his offer of queenship, and laments over her dying mate until her grief's power heats Sakka's throne, and the god, as a brahmin, heals the wound with heavenly water and bids the pair keep to their mountain.
summary.zh: 菩薩生為山林精靈緊那羅，與妻月女居月山，以歌相娛。王獨自狩獵，貪其妻之美，射傷緊那羅。月女咒詛王，拒其后位之誘，抱垂死之夫哀泣，悲慟之力熱帝釋座；帝釋化婆羅門以天水愈其傷，囑二神自此勿下山。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this in the palace of Rāhula's mother, praising her constancy: she had clothed herself in yellow at the news of his ordination, given up garlands, and refused the gifts of other kings. "Not now only, but even when born as an animal, she was faithful and mine alone." Of old, when Brahmadatta was king in Benares, the Great Being was born a fairy or kinnara in the Himalaya, and his wife was named Canda; the two dwelt together on a silver mountain called Canda-pabbata, the Mountain of the Moon. The king of Benares had committed his government to his ministers and gone alone into the Himalayas in yellow robes, armed with the five weapons. There the kinnaras came down for the hot season, crowned with flowers and clothed in flower-gauze, singing in honey voices.

On a sandy spot white as a silver plate they spread a couch of flowers, and the fairy played upon a piece of bamboo and sang while Canda waved her soft hands and danced beside him, singing too. The king caught the sound, stole close, and stood watching from a hiding place; he fell in love with the female fairy and resolved to shoot the husband and live there with the wife. He shot the fairy Canda, who lamented in four stanzas as his blood flowed and his breath went—yet each stanza turned not on his own pain but on his yearning for her sorrow. Lying upon his couch of flowers he lost consciousness; the king stood where he was. Canda, rapt in her own delight, did not know he was wounded till she saw the blood oozing from the wound's mouth; then, unable to bear the pain of sorrow, she cried out loud, and the king came out and showed himself.

Thinking him the brigand who had slain her husband, she fled trembling to the hill-top and denounced the king in five stanzas, praying that the woe that wrung her heart be repaid upon his mother and his wife, who would mourn her lord and son for this deed done for lust. "Weep not nor grieve: the woodland dark has blinded you, I ween; a royal house shall honour thee, and thou shalt be my queen," the king answered. "No! I will surely slay myself! thine I will never be, who slew my husband innocent and all for lust of me," she roared like a lion; and his passion left him, and he let her go to the Himalaya. Then she came down, embraced the Great Being, carried him to the hill-top, and laid his head on her lap, making her moan in twelve stanzas over every hill and glen and flower that would see her no more; and taunting the gods for leaving a righteous world ungoverned, she so wrought on them that Sakka's throne grew hot with the power of her pain.

Sakka, pondering, discovered the cause, and in the form of a brahmin approached with a water-pot and sprinkled the Great Being with water. On the instant the poison ceased to act, his colour returned, and he knew not so much as where the wound had been: the Great Being stood up quite well. Canda fell at the brahmin's feet and sang his praise for restoring her well-loved husband with the elixir of life; Sakka bade them go no more down from the Mountain of the Moon among the paths of men, and returned to his own place. And Canda said to her husband, "Why stay here in danger, my lord? come, let us go to the Mountain of the Moon, where the lovely rivers flow, all o'ergrown with flowers; there for ever, while the breeze whispers in a thousand trees, charm with talk the happy hours." The Master identified the Birth: Anuruddha was the king, Rāhula's mother was Canda, and the fairy was himself.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Indapatta, capital of the Kuru kingdom, and Mount Nanda in the Himalaya (symbolic pin for the mountain)
region.zh: 俱盧國因陀羅波達城；雪山楠達山洞（山為象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: King Koravya's lavish almsgiving profits him nothing, for every recipient is wicked; his wise minister Vidhura catalogues ten kinds of men who are brahmins in name only—herb-sellers, bell-ringing servants, importunate beggars, wood-cutters, traders, cattle-dealers, sacrificers who slaughter, caravan guards, hunters, and scapegoats beneath the royal bed—and finds the only worthy recipients in five hundred Silent Buddhas of Mount Nanda, whom the king feasts for seven days.
summary.zh: 憍羅耶王廣行布施而無所得，蓋受者皆無德。賢臣毘提羅歷數十種徒有其名之婆羅門——賣藥者、鳴鈴僕役、強乞者、樵夫、商販、賣女者、殺生祭司、護商者、獵人、代王受垢者——並指唯有楠達山洞中五百獨覺佛堪受供養。王齋供七日，所施衣物隨之凌空而返。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this at Jetavana of a gift incomparable, given by the king of Kosala with discrimination to the holiest of the Brethren; "wise men of old, ere yet the Buddha had arisen, even they gave with discrimination." Of old, in the kingdom of Kuru and the city of Indapatta, reigned king Koravya, whose adviser in things temporal and spiritual was the wise Vidhura. The king's great almsgiving set all India in commotion, yet among all who received and enjoyed his gifts not one kept so much as the Five Virtues—all were wicked to a man—and the king's giving brought him no satisfaction. Desiring to give to the virtuous, he took counsel with Vidhura: seek me brahmins good, in whom much wisdom lies, men free from deeds of evil lust, that they may eat my food.

"'Tis hard to find such holy men," answered Vidhura, and in question and answer with the king he distinguished ten kinds who are brahmins in name only: some carry sacks of healing herbs, bathe, and recite magic spells—physician-like; some ring bells before the king and drive his chariot—servant-like; some with waterpot and crooked staff follow towns crying for gifts—importunate as tax-men; some, long-nailed and dirty, hew wood—mere hewers; some traffic in fruit and honey—merchants; some follow trade and sell their daughters in marriage—like Vessa; some as chaplains tell fortunes and slaughter many beasts at village invitations—like butchers; some stand armed with sword and shield before merchants' caravans—like bandits; some trap fish and hare in woodland huts—hunters; and some lie beneath the royal bed at the soma-sacrifice to catch the washing of the king's sins—like barbers. "These have no right to such a name: lost is their brahminhood," said the king to each in turn.

But there are brahmins, too, said Vidhura, men very wise and good, free from the deeds of evil lust, who eat one meal of rice and never touch strong drink—they dwell in the further Himalaya, in a cave of Mount Nanda. Then Vidhura bade the king proclaim through the city that all should adorn it, give alms, keep the holy-day vows, and pledge themselves to virtue; and himself, taking the vows, cast eight handfuls of flowers into the air, calling to mind the virtues of the Silent Buddhas: let the five hundred Pacceka Buddhas of the cave of Mount Nanda to-morrow partake of our food. The flowers fell upon them in their far dwelling; they understood, judged Vidhura no mean creature—one having the seed of a Buddha within him, to be a Buddha in this very cycle—and accepted the invitation.

Next day they flew through the air from Lake Anotatta and descended in the royal courtyard; the king and Vidhura received their bowls, seated them on the terrace, gave them the gift-water, and served them with delightful food for seven days, presenting many gifts; on the seventh day he gave them all the requisites, and they gave thanks and flew back to their cave, the requisites going with them. Of that time Ananda was the king, and the wise Vidhura was the Master himself.

title.en: Haṃsa-Jātaka (The Golden Goose and the Faithful Friend)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Benares and Mount Cittakūṭa (symbolic pin for the mountain)
region.zh: 波羅奈與質多羅山（山為象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Queen Khema dreams of hearing a Golden Goose preach the Law, and the king builds a lake to snare one; the goose-king Dhatarattha is caught, and his captain Sumukha, though free, returns to share his prisoner's fate, 'I'll not leave you... will either live or die.' The moved hunter frees and heals the royal bird, and the goose preaches all night to the king until the queen's craving is appeased, then flies home.
summary.zh: 吉祥王后夢聞金鵝說法，王遂鑿湖設網捕鵝。鵝王法螺賢落網，其部屬善友雖可脫身仍返相伴，誓同生共死。獵人感動，縱之療傷；鵝王入宮為王說法通宵，王后願足，雙鵝飛還山中。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this in the Bamboo Grove of Elder Ananda's renunciation of his life for the Teacher's sake—"not the first time." Of old, in Benares reigned a king named Bahuputtaka, Father of Many Sons, and his queen consort was Khema. The Great Being then dwelt on Mount Cittakūṭa, chief of ninety thousand wild geese, come to life as a golden goose. The queen dreamed a dream and told the king she had conceived a woman's craving to hear a Golden Goose discourse of the Law; told that such creatures lived on Cittakūṭa, the king made a lake which he called Khema, planted it with all manner of food-corn, had immunity proclaimed daily in the four quarters, and sent a hunter to catch the geese. In a snare set among the crops the Great Being was caught; the goose flock fled in three divisions, but Sumukha their chief captain, missing his king, came back.

Hanging in the noose, the goose-king tested his friend: "There go the birds, the ruddy geese, all overcome with fear: O golden-yellow Sumukha, depart! what want you here? ... Fly, noble bird! with prisoners no fellowship can be." "No, I'll not leave you, Royal Goose, when trouble draweth nigh: but stay I will, and by your side will either live or die," Sumukha answered, sitting on the mud. "'Twas but to put you to the test I bade you fly away," said the king of the geese. Up came the huntsman at top speed; Sumukha flew to meet him and declared the virtues of the royal bird, and the hunter's heart was softened. Asked how the birds, treading unfooted ways, had failed to spy the snare, the Great Being answered, "When life is coming to an end, and death's hour draws anigh, though you may close upon it come, nor trap nor snare you spy." Asked why, though free, he stayed with a prisoner, Sumukha said, "He is my comrade, friend, and king, dear as my life is he: forsake him—no, I never will, until death calls for me."

The hunter thought that if he harmed such virtuous creatures the earth would gape and swallow him—what care he for the king's reward?—and set them free, drawing the royal bird from the stick, washing the blood from him, and setting the dislocated sinews, so that by the Great Being's perfections the foot became whole on the instant and not a mark showed. The goose-king chose rather to go to the town: the hunter would be rewarded, the queen's craving appeased, Sumukha's friendship made known, and by his wisdom he should receive the lake Khema as a free gift. So the hunter carried them on his carrying-pole to the king, who placed both geese on a golden perch, fed them with honey and fried grain, and held out his hands, praying them to speak of the Law. The goose catechised the king on his health, wealth, righteous rule, unblemished court, far-off foes, queen, and sons—"sons I have of fame, five score and one; tell them their duty: they'll not leave your good advice undone"—and then admonished him in five stanzas.

"He that puts off until too late the effort to do good, though nobly bred, with virtue dowered, yet sinks beneath the flood; his knowledge fades... as one moonblind at night sees all things swollen twice their size with his imperfect sight. Who sees the truth in falsity no wisdom gains at all, as on a rugged mountain-path the deer will often fall. If any strong courageous man loves virtue, follows right, though but a low-born churl, he burns like bonfires in the night. By using this similitude all wisdom's truths explain: cherish your sons till wise they grow, like seedlings in the rain." So the Great Being discoursed to the king the livelong night; the queen's craving was appeased, and by sunrise, having established the king in the virtues of kings and exhorted him to vigilance, the goose flew out of the northern window with Sumukha and away to Cittakūṭa. The Master identified the Birth: the huntsman was Channa, Sāriputta the king, Ānanda was Sumukha, and he himself was the Goose King.

title.en: Aḷambusā-Jātaka (The Nymph and the Young Ascetic)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Himalaya hermitage and Indra's heaven (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雪山精舍與天界（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: The ascetic Isisinga, born of a doe that drank water mixed with a brahmin's seed, is warned by his dying father against women, yet the sheer power of his austerity so heats Sakka's throne that the god sends the nymph Aḷambusā to break his virtue. Her praise-song lures him to seize her in flight, and he lies lost in her arms three years; waking, he laments his broken vows, resumes his meditation, forgives her, and she begs a boon never to tempt a saint again.
summary.zh: 獨覺之子伊 西 行伽 乃母鹿飲仙人之水而孕所生；父臨終誡勿近女色，然其苦行威德熱帝釋座，神遣天女阿蘭浮沙誘之。天女讚歌相誘、佯逃相引，仙人執其髮而失定，沉眠其懷三年。醒後慟悔，重入禪定，赦其罪；天女求得「永不誘聖者」之願。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka paralleling the Rishyasringa episode of the Hindu Ramayana and the Barlaam-and-Josaphat tradition; retold freely as scripture of a living tradition; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of a Brother tempted to discontent by the wife of his unregenerate days—owing to her, said the Master, he once fell from mystic meditation and lay three years lost and distracted. Of old, in the reign of Brahmadatta in Benares, a doe ate grass and drank water mingled with a brahmin ascetic's seed, became enamoured, and bore him a man child, Isisinga, whom the ascetic reared with a father's affection, admitted to holy orders, and warned: "In this Himalaya country are women as fair as these flowers: they bring utter destruction on all that fall into their power." Soon after he was destined for the Brahma world; but the son, indulging in mystic meditation with all his senses mortified, became an ascetic so severe that the abode of Sakka was shaken, and Sakka, fearing to be displaced, searched the twenty-five millions of his handmaids for one equal to the task of breaking the saint's virtue, and found none but Aḷambusā.

"Go, Temptress, ever dog his steps, for holy sage is he, and, seeking ever highest bliss, still triumphs over me," said Sakka; Aḷambusā asked why she alone of all the nymphs of Nandana, and feared the hell that waits on wrongs to saints, yet went at the god's behest. At break of day, before the sun was astir, she drew near to Isisinga as he swept out his cell. The ascetic questioned her—"Who art thou, like to lightning flash, or bright as morning star?"—and sang her praises from head to foot: slender waist, eyes like guñja berries, teeth like pearls, the triple line on her neck. While he spoke she was silent, and reading how disturbed his state of mind had grown, she answered, "Heaven bless thee, Kassapa, my friend, the time is past and gone for idle questions such as these—for are we not alone?—come let us in thy hermitage embracing haste to prove the thousand joys well known to all the votaries of love."

Then, with a woman's cunning, she made as if to run away; the ascetic cried "She is off," intercepted her with motion swift as air, and seized her by the hair. Just where he stood the lovely maid embraced him in her arms, and his virtue fell before the magic of her charms; in thought she flew to Indra's throne in Nandana afar, and the god sent a golden car with trappings spread. There the saint lay in her arms for many a long day: three years passed over his head as though it were a moment's space. At last he woke, saw the green trees and the cuckoo-crying groves, and wept bitterly: "I make no offering, raise no hymn; no sacrifice is here. Who can my tempter be, who by foul practice has overcome all sense of right in me, even as a ship with precious freight is swallowed in the sea?" Told that she was sent by king Sakka, he called to mind his father's warning—"Women are fair as lotus flower; beware, good youth, their subtle power"—and lamented that he had let his wise old father's words pass unheeded.

"Accursed be the life of old: henceforth I'll do as I am told; far better death itself to face, than be again in such a case." So he forsook sensual desire and entered upon mystic meditation; and Aḷambusā, seeing his steadfast power and courage return, became terrified and asked his forgiveness, kneeling to embrace his feet: "A mighty work I wrought, when heaven itself and gods of fame trembled with fear to hear thy name." "I pardon thee, fair lady; go, as thou wilt," he said, blessing the Thirty-three and her; and saluting him, she mounted the golden car and sped away like blazing torch or lightning flash. Sakka, glad at heart, cried "No boon can I deny," and Aḷambusā asked but this: "Let me ne'er tempt a saint again to violate his vow." Of that time the nymph was the Brother's former wife, Isisinga the backsliding Brother, and the great saint his father the Master himself.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Rajagaha in Magadha; river Kannapennā and the naga palace
region.zh: 摩竭陀王舍城；迦那奔那河與龍宮

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Prince Duyyodhana of Magadha, coveting the glory of the naga king Saṅkhapāla who visits his ascetic father, gives alms and keeps the holy days until reborn as a serpent king—then, finding the naga world no place for purity, keeps fast-days on an ant-heap, offering his body to all comers. Sixteen hunters stake and drag him; the landowner Āḷāra buys him free, is rewarded with a year in the naga palace, and returns to preach the vanity of desires to the king of Benares.
summary.zh: 摩竭陀王子睹龍王榮耀而生欣羨，廣行布施、持齋布薩，感生龍界為王；然悟龍身非清淨之地，遂於蟻垤持齋，自許其身任人取用。十六獵人戳刺拖曳；地主阿羅以牛與金贖之，獲龍宮一年之報，歸而向波羅奈王宣說欲之無常。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master, expressing approval of lay folk who kept holy days, told them that wise men of old gave up the great glory of the Naga world to observe those vows. Of old, a king of Magadha reigned in Rajagaha, and the Bodhisatta, born as prince Duyyodhana, was installed in the kingdom while his father took up the religious life in the park. Thrice daily the son visited the father, whose honor and profit thus grew so great that the old king could not even prepare for mystic meditation, and stole away without a word beyond the borders, to a hut by Mount Candaka at the bend of the river Kannapennā, where it issues from lake Saṅkhapāla. There the naga king Saṅkhapāla, issuing from the river with his company, would visit the ascetic and hear the Law. The son, seeking his father, came upon the serpent's departing magnificence and conceived a longing for the Naga world; ever after he kept the moral law and the holy days, gave alms at the four gates, and at his death was reborn in the Naga world as king Saṅkhapāla.

In time he grew sick of that magnificence and longed to be born as a man, for dwelling in the Naga world his observance of the holy days was not a success and he deteriorated in morals. Leaving the Naga world he coiled round an ant-hill between the high road and a narrow path, resolved to keep the holy day, saying, "Let those that want my skin or want my skin and flesh, let them, I say, take it all," and lay there on the fourteenth and fifteenth of the half-month, returning to the palace on the first day of each fortnight. One day sixteen men of a neighboring village, hunting in vain for flesh, saw him and resolved to kill and eat the snake-king; fearing his size, they took stakes, and the Bodhisatta made his body big as a trough-shaped canoe, beautiful as a jasmine wreath, and tucked his head into his hood, resolved that when they struck him he would not open his eyes or regard them with anger.

They seized him by the tail, dragged him, wounded him in eight places with sharp stakes and thrust black bamboo sticks, thorns and all, into the open wounds; strung him by cords through eight piercings; and when his head drooped, pierced his nostrils with a slender stake and raised his head by a cord. Never once from the moment of the first wound did he open his eyes or look on them with anger. Then Āḷāra, a landowner of Mithila journeying with five hundred wagons, gave all sixteen an ox apiece, a handful of golden coins, garments, and ornaments for their wives, and so got them to release him. The Bodhisatta returned to the Naga palace, issued forth with a great retinue, took Āḷāra with him, and for a whole year satisfied him with heavenly delights, three hundred naga maidens serving, until Āḷāra asked instead for the requisites of the ascetic life and departed to the Himalaya.

In time the ascetic came to Benares and lodged in the king's park; charmed, the king asked why one of such noble presence had renounced earth's joys. Alara told him how on a trading venture he had met the captured snake, bought him with oxen and gold, and been led to a dwelling of gold and gems thronged with nymphs; and how the serpent-king, questioned, confessed that the mansion was owed to his own good actions as king Duyyodhana of Magadha—he supplied meat and drink religiously, and made his house an inn where sages refreshed themselves—and that he had suffered hurt on the holy days by no overmastering dread but in the cause of goodness, whose bounds like the seashore are never transgressed: "Nowhere but in the world of men, I ween, may purity and self-restraint be seen: if only once midst men I draw my breath, I'll put an end to further birth and death." The king vowed to perform all deeds of piety; the ascetic passed to the Brahma heaven, and the Master identified the Birth: the father-ascetic was Kassapa, the king of Benares was Ananda, Alara was Sariputta, and Sankhapala was himself.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Sudassana city (the Benares of that birth) and the Himalaya hermitage
region.zh: 須達沙城（彼世之波羅奈）與雪山精舍

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: King Sutasoma, whose face is glorious as the full moon, orders his barber to tell him when a grey hair appears—and on receiving that single grey hair renounces his vast kingdom over the wailing of his mother, father, seven hundred wives and his pregnant queen. He bribes the nurse to take his clinging seven-year-old son away, cuts his top-knot on the Palace of Flowers before the people, and leads a company covering twelve leagues to a hermitage built for him by Sakka's command.
summary.zh: 蘇達沙王面如滿月，命理髮師見白髮即告；得一莖白髮遂捨大國。母、父、七百妃與懷孕王后皆泣勸不果，並賄乳母抱走其七歲稚子；於花宮頂當眾斷髮髻，率十二由旬之眾往帝釋所命營建之精舍。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this concerning the perfect exercise of self-abnegation. Of old, what is now Benares was a city called Sudassana, and king Brahmadatta's chief consort bore the Bodhisatta, whose face was glorious as the full moon, so that he was named Somakumāra, and from his fondness for soma juice, Sutasoma. Educated at Taxila, he ruled a vast dominion with sixteen thousand wives, Candadevī at their head, and a numerous family. But he grew discontented with domestic life and told his barber, "When you see a grey hair on my head, you are to tell me." In time the barber, with golden tweezers, laid a grey hair in his hand. "My body is a prey to old age," cried the king, and descending from the terrace he seated himself on a throne before the people, summoned his eighty thousand councillors and sixty thousand brahmins, and announced, "A grey hair has appeared on my head; I am an old man, and you are to know that I am become an ascetic."

Each counsellor felt the arrow quiver in his heart: remember thy seven hundred wives, O king—what will become of them? "Their sorrows soon another will console, for they are young in years and fair to see; but I am bent upon a heavenly goal." His mother came in hot haste lamenting the day that hailed her mother of such a son; his father asked what Law led him to quit kingdom and home with old parents left alone; and he, for answer, showed them the Law and held his peace. His seven hundred wives threw themselves at his feet weeping that his heart must break or pity unknown; "My heart in sorrow may not break, though I feel pity for your pain, but holy orders I must take, that I may heavenly bliss attain." His queen consort, heavy with child and near her time, begged him stay till the babe was born; "The hour of thy delivery is nigh; until the babe is born, I'll stay with thee; then will I leave the royal imp and fly far from the world a holy monk to be."

His elder son asked whom he must impiously slay for his mother's tears; but the younger, seven years old, comforted them both, and coming down from the tower clasped his father by the neck: "I too will hold thee by the hand, nor let thee go against our will." "This child is a source of danger to me," thought the Bodhisatta, and looking at the nurse, "Good nurse, behold this jewel ornament: this is yours: only take away the child, that he be not a hindrance to me." She took the bribe and led the boy away. His commander offered the subdued world; the rich merchant Kulavaddhana offered wealth beyond reckoning; his brother Somadatta begged to follow him into the hermit's cell, and was refused. "Like water through a sieve, our day so brief alas! fast slips away," the Great Being taught the weeping people, and then, on the topmost storey of the Palace of Flowers, cut off his top-knot with a sword and cried, "I am now nothing to you; choose ye a king of your own," casting turban and all into the crowd, who rolled on the ground in lamentation under the rising dust-cloud.

A barber shaved his hair and beard; he fastened an earthen bowl on his shoulder, took the mendicant's staff, and stepped out into the street unrecognised; his wives found only the bundle of his adornments, and the city cried, "King Sutasoma, sad to tell, has left his throne for hermit cell, and, clad in yellow, goes his way like some lone elephant astray." The people followed him and the whole city emptied, until the company covered twelve leagues. Sakka ordered Vissakamma to build a hermitage thirty leagues long and five broad; the Great Being entered by the path, was first ordained, admitted the rest to orders until a space of thirty leagues was filled, and if any false thought arose in any mind he would come through the air and admonish them: "Call not to mind love's sports of yore... indulge without or stint or stay good will to men by night and day, so shall ye win the angel home." The saints abiding by his admonition were destined to the Brahma world; the elder son was Sariputta, the younger Rahula, prince Somadatta was Ananda, and king Sutasoma was the Master.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Sakka stops the rain for three years to break the austere virtue of the young ascetic Isisinga, and tells the starving king of Benares that only his daughter Nalinikā can do it. Sent into the forest with ministers and elephants, the princess disguises herself as an ascetic youth playing with a ball that always returns to her hand, seduces the innocent boy, and slips away before his father returns; the rain falls that very day, and the father's rebuke restores his son's meditation.
summary.zh: 帝釋為破伊 西 行伽 少年仙人之淨行而止雨三年，語飢困之波羅奈王：唯王女娜律尼迦能成此事。公主隨眾入山，偽裝仙人少年，弄一手擲必回之球誘惑天真的小仙人，旋即遁去；當日雨降。父歸斥其為妖變所惑，其禪定復得。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of a Brother tempted by the wife of his unregenerate days—of old it was owing to her that he fell from mystic meditation and was mightily destroyed. Of old, a brahmin of the North, trained in all the arts, became an ascetic in the Himalayas; exactly as in the Aḷambusā Birth a doe conceived by him and brought forth a son called Isisinga. His father admitted him to holy orders, had him instructed in the rites inducing mystic meditation, and the youth soon enjoyed the bliss of ecstasy, an ascetic of such severe austerity that the abode of Sakka was shaken. Sakka discovered the cause, and for three years stopped the rain over the kingdom of Kāsi: the country was scorched, no crops came to perfection, and the people gathered in the palace yard to reproach the king, who, though he took the moral vows and fasted, could bring down no rain.

At midnight Sakka stood in mid-air in the illuminated royal chamber and told the king that in the Himalaya dwelt the ascetic Isisinga, who constantly, when it began to rain, looked up at the sky in a rage, and so the rain ceased. "Should his virtue be broken down, it will rain." "But who is able to overcome his virtue?" "Your daughter, Sire, Nalinikā can do it." Though these were things not to be spoken of in words, the king, for the protection of his realm, talked with his daughter and sent her away with his ministers, elephants and footmen. Pitching camp at the frontier, they had the princess conveyed by foresters' paths to the edge of the hermitage; and while the Bodhisatta was gone into the forest for wild fruits, they surrounded the cloister, disguised the princess as an ascetic youth in a beautiful bark garment with all manner of ornaments, and sent her in playing with a painted ball tied to a string, while they stood on guard without.

Isisinga, seeing her come, was terrified and hid in his hut; but she played with her ball at the door, her lovely limbs exposed to his gaze, and when he broke forth asking what fruit of what tree this might be that however far 'tis tossed still returns again and never more is lost, she answered falsely of Mount Gandhamādana, whose trees bear such fruit. Believing her an ascetic, he offered seat and food; and being an ingenuous youth who had never seen a woman before, he was led to believe her extraordinary story, and through her seductions his virtue was overcome and his meditation broken off. When he asked by what road she had come, she described her hermit cot by the Kāusikī north of the Himalayan snows; but fearing his father's return, she planned her escape—"Alas! I fear I may no longer stay, but many a royal saint lives on the way: ask one of them to point you out the road"—and left the youth wistfully looking after her. That very day Sakka, delighted, caused rain to fall throughout the whole kingdom.

But directly she had left, a fever seized the boy, and he lay groaning in his hut where his returning father found him. Then the boy poured out his lovesick lament over the fair youth—the smoothed dark hair, the curvéd rings at either ear, the voice softer than the cuckoo's—and begged to be told where this holy youth dwelt, or he would lie down and die at the door. The Great Being knew at once that through some woman his son had lost his virtue, and rebuked him: friendships exist and then they cease; just as a flood sweeps off the ripened corn, so will the power of virtue be overborne by such a meeting—"Demons there be that through the wide earth run in varied form disguised. Beware, my son!" The terrified youth thought, "She was a female yakkha, he says," and asked his father's pardon, promising never to leave the spot; his father comforted him and proclaimed the four Perfect States, and the son walked therein and once more developed mystic meditation. Of that time the wife of his unregenerate days was Nalinika, the backsliding Brother was Isisinga, and the Master was the father.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Rajagaha, Benares royal park and palace
region.zh: 王舍城；波羅奈御苑與王宮

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: King Arindama forgets his friend Sonaka for forty years, singing his reward song through all Benares, while Sonaka, a withered sal-leaf falling before him, becomes a Silent Buddha. Fifty years on he teaches the reward-song's refrain to a wood-gathering boy, who sings it back before the king; led to the park, the king insults the shaven recluse and is rebuked, then hears the parable of the crow that feasted on a floating carcass until the Ganges swept it to the sea, and renounces his throne the same day.
summary.zh: 阿林達摩王四十年來遍唱「見我故友者賞千頂冠」之歌，而蘇那迦見落葉悟無常，已成獨覺佛。後教拾柴小兒續唱其歌詞；王循歌至御苑，斥剃髮行者為可憐蟲而遭反詰；聞「烏鴉食浮屍隨流至海」之喻，當日捨王位。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this concerning the Perfection of Renunciation: "not now only, but of old also the Tathāgata verily left the world and made the Great Renunciation." Of old, the Magadha king reigned in Rajagaha, and on the day the Bodhisatta was born to his chief queen as prince Arindama, a son was born to the royal chaplain and named young Sonaka. The two boys grew up alike as twins and studied at Taxila; wandering to Benares they lodged in the royal park, and at a brahmins' almsgiving the seats assigned them—white cloth for one, red woollen rug for the other—told Sonaka that that day his friend would be made king of Benares and would offer him the post of commander-in-chief. On the seventh day after the king's death the festal car stopped at the park gate for any worthy man to mount; the chaplain sprinkled the Bodhisatta king on the spot and led him into the city with a vast escort, and in the greatness of his glory the king forgot all about Sonaka.

But when the king was gone, Sonaka sat again on the stone seat, and a withered leaf of a sal tree fell from its stalk in front of him. "Even as this leaf, so will my body fall into decay," he cried, and acquiring supernatural insight by reflecting on the impermanence of all things he attained that instant to the state of a Silent Buddha—his layman's marks vanishing, the ascetic's appearing—and set out for the cave of Nandamūla. The king, after forty years, remembered Sonaka, and offered a thousand pieces to whoever should see him with his own eyes and a hundred to whoever should hear of him, singing his aspiration: "A thousand crowns for one that sees my friend and playmate dear; a hundred lo! I give if one of Sonaka should hear." The song passed from mouth to mouth through harem, city and country till all sang it. Fifty years on, Sonaka, moved by the king's longing, came back through the air and taught the refrain to a seven-year-old boy gathering sticks in the park.

Bathed and dressed in his best, the boy had a drum beaten through the city, and before all the people the king sang first and the boy—five tangled locks he wore—answered: "The thousand give to me who saw, who heard a hundred more: I'll tell thee news of Sonaka, thy playfellow of yore. Within this realm, in thine own park is many a big sal tree... and at their foot lo! Sonaka in meditation lies, filled with the Arhat's holy calm, when human passion dies." The king started in full force and found his friend at rest, passionless and saintly; but given up to evil passion, he insulted him without saluting: "His parents dead, with shaven head, clad in monk's robe I see, a wretched Brother in a trance, stretched here beneath this tree." "He is no wretched wight who in his every action, Sire, has aye attained to right; nay rather wretched those who right neglect and practise ill, for evil doer evil doom is destined to fulfil."

Proving himself king of Kasi, Arindama asked if the sage had met with anything deserving blame, and Sonaka told the eight blessings of the homeless monk; but the king cut him short: "I have no need of monkish blessings... how to gain both worlds at once, to me, I prithee, tell." Then came the parable: a foolish crow, seeing a vast carcass floating past on the Ganges' tide, boarded it for goodly store of food and stayed eating and drinking till the river swept him headlong to the sea, where the monster fish came ravening round and devoured him. "So thou and all that greedily pleasures of sense pursue are deemed as wise as was this crow, till ye all lusts eschew." "In pity once, nay even twice, utter the warning word, but keep not on repeating it like a slave before his lord"—and the sage vanished through the air. The king resolved, "To-morrow one may die, who knows? I'll be ordained to-day," gave his sixty thousand villages, elephants, horses, cars and maidens to his son Dighavu, and was destined for the Brahma world; of that time the son was young Rahula and the king the Master.

title.en: Mahāsutasoma-Jātaka (The Ogre-King and the Four Verses)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Indapatta in the Kuru country and the man-eater's forest (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧國因陀羅波達與食人者之林（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: The king of Benares, given corpse-meat by his cook, conceives an incurable craving for human flesh, is exposed by his commander and banished, and becomes a man-eater who captures a hundred and one kings to sacrifice to the tree-nymph who healed his wound. Warned by that nymph, he seizes prince Sutasoma, his old teacher; released to hear four stanzas worth a hundred pieces each, Sutasoma returns under oath and wins four boons—life for the man-eater, the kings' lives, their release, and the end of cannibalism—till gods and men applaud the conversion.
summary.zh: 波羅奈王誤食人肉而生難遏之嗜，事發遭逐，成為食人魔王；為償樹神愈傷之願，捕一百零一王以祭。樹神勸其先擄舊師蘇達沙摩王子；釋之令聽四偈，王子誓言既立乃返，索四願——魔王長壽、諸王不死、各歸其國、戒食人肉——天人同聲喝采。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka containing cannibalism and vivid hell-threats; retold freely as scripture of a living tradition; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this concerning the Elder Angulimala, the blood-stained robber whom he converted without violence: "I also tamed him when I was living in a previous stage of existence." Of old, king Koravya reigned in Indapatta of the Kuru country, and the Bodhisatta was born his son, Sutasoma, sent with one hundred and one princes to the same world-famed teacher; Sutasoma, senior pupil, took prince Brahmadatta of Benares for his private pupil, and on parting bade them all keep the Uposatha vows and abstain from taking life on the new- and full-moon days. But the king of Benares never ate his rice meal without meat; when the palace dogs ate the meat kept for a fast-day, the cook, fearing death, served flesh cut from a corpse in the cemetery, and the king, thrilled to the seven thousand nerves of taste—human flesh had been his food as a yakkha in the birth before—commanded the cook to furnish it always: first from the prisons, then by a baited purse of a thousand pieces, then by murdering passers-by at the night-watches. Caught at last with his basket of flesh, the cook accused his master before commander-in-chief Kalahatthi, and the king confessed.

"Sire, do not this thing; eat not the flesh of men... if you do not cease from it, you will destroy both yourself and your realm." The commander told him of the monster fish Ananda, who tasted one of the fish that paid him court and then devoured his subjects until, madness and hunger driving him, he seized his own tail and was eaten piecemeal by the fish he had spared; but the king answered with his own examples—the lad who died for want of a third rose-apple, the brahmin's son ruined by a first taste of liquor, the gentleman who pined away crying for an Apsarā—and the golden geese who, eating the eggs, goslings and flesh of their own kin through a five-month rain, grew so feeble that the cave-spider sucked their blood one by one till their family was extinct. The citizens rose and would hear nothing: "Have him expelled from his kingdom." The king begged only his sword, his cooking vessel and his cook, and went into the forest, where he waylaid travellers, crying "Here am I, the man-eating robber!"—till he killed even the cook who failed him, and lived alone.

A wealthy brahmin's caravan paid for convoy through the forest, yet the man-eater seized him from his white-oxen carriage and carried him off head downward, lamed by an acacia splinter. At the foot of his banyan tree he prayed the tree-nymph: heal my wound within seven days and I will sacrifice the blood and inwards of a hundred and one princes of all India. His wound healed, his old comrade of yakkha days taught him a spell of strength and wind-swift speed, and within seven days he found and captured a hundred and one kings, hanging them by cords through their pierced palms on the banyan tree. But Sutasoma he spared—"Sutasoma was my private teacher: let not India be altogether desolate"—and when he lit the fire and sat sharpening the stake, the tree-nymph, fearing the coming slaughter, sought the Four Great Kings and Sakka, who could not stop him but named the one who could: prince Sutasoma of Indapatta. Disguised as an ascetic, she let herself be chased three leagues, stood fast at the word "Stand!"—"I am standing; do you too try and stand"—revealed herself blazing in the sky, and counseled: bid him first bring Sutasoma, then offer his sacrifice.

Learning by the stars when Sutasoma would bathe in the royal tank, the man-eater lurked in the water and took him from the midst of his army. "I weep not for myself or wife or child or realm," said the prince, "but for a promise: once to a brahmin I my word did plight; that word I fain would keep, and then, my honour saved, return to thee." "No man escaped from death returns to his foe," laughed the robber, till Sutasoma swore a kshatriya's oath and the man-eater let him go. Sutasoma heard the four stanzas the brahmin Nanda had brought from Kassapa Buddha, and went back with death written on his forehead. Awestruck, the man-eater begged to hear them, and offered a boon for each stanza; the prince chose: long life for the man-eater himself; the hundred kings not eaten; each king restored to his realm; and abstinence from human flesh. The ogre wept and yielded at last, bowing at the prince's feet and taking the five moral laws at his hands; the deities of earth roared applause, and the man-eater went with Sutasoma and loosed the kings. Of old the Master, as Sutasoma, tamed this man-eater.
